A previous side chat wrote: 
```plaintext
I updated the live experiment docs to make SAM3.1 the preferred development mask candidate, while keeping its predictions labeled as pseudo-labels. I did not overwrite the cached masks: the existing cache’s provenance is unresolved, and replacing it would change historical measurements. The only SAM masks available cover 16 frames of one scene and include players, not rackets.
```



We have established sam3.1 masks are the best we can get, so we need to make sure the dataset is using them, and replace the current ones with these, so that when we train new models, they have a better quality prior. 



The previous side chat also reported:
```plaintext
The racket is visible outside the player masks. I couldn’t run the separate racket prompts or generate masks for the rest of the dataset: this execution context has no CUDA device, even through the GPU-access attempt. So there are no new racket masks to compare yet.
```



We need to run sam 3.1 once for players, and once for rackets, so that these masks can be used to generate crops of the players, that we can then pass to dw-pose or yolo to extract players keypoints, and generate crops of the rackets, that we can use to generate their keypoints from some heuristic that we might have already defined, or if not, we must define.



Then, we can pass the keypoints as metadata, and we need to train models that take those keypoints and generate the initial objects. For players, we can use pre-existing models such as animate-anyone or MTTF, while for rackets we need to train our own models (Controlnet, SPADE, etc), like we did before, but now on better inputs. And we can even train a joint model of racket and player.



To this prompt, side chat 1, which is now expired, responded:
```markdown
The GPU is available on the host: the RTX A6000 was idle, and the pinned SAM3.1 checkpoint loaded successfully. The existing player smoke already covers 16 frames. I ran a separate “tennis racket” prompt on that same window: it produced masks for two tracks initially, but both tracks were present together in only 12 of 16 frames; one disappeared for the final four. Runtime was 30.6 seconds, with 19.7 GiB peak reserved GPU memory. This is a useful prompt test, but it does not establish masks reliable enough for a dataset-wide replacement.

The run artifacts are the [result ledger](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/outputs/journal-20260926/sam31-racket-prompt-smoke16-run1/result.json), [preregistration](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/manifests/journal_20260926_sam31_racket_prompt_smoke16.json), and [predicted racket masks](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/outputs/journal-20260926/sam31-racket-prompt-smoke16-run1/predicted_racket_masks.npz). No training data or prior evaluation masks were overwritten.
I found existing racket inputs in the dataset: per-frame metadata has racket_bbox_crop and four racket_mask_points, and tracks have pose_racket condition images. The current codec’s racket heuristic is also defined, but it emits a convex hull anchored to the nearest player wrist; it does not produce racket keypoints. The meaning and provenance of the stored p1–p4 points still need checking before treating them as semantic racket joints.
The next step is to use those per-frame racket boxes or points to guide SAM, then verify continuity and inspect the resulting crops before building a versioned SAM training view. Player DWPose/YOLO extraction and model training should follow that dataset pass. Full-dataset replacement, keypoint generation, and training remain undone.
```



At the same time, side chat 2 was working on dw-pose, and reported:
```markdown
Implemented the motion-codec changes in an isolated checkout at `/tmp/pointstream-motion-contract-20260926` on branch `codex/motion-contract-20260926`, based on the same commit as the main checkout. I left the shared checkout untouched.

- **GPU integration:** Added and preregistered a bounded 16-frame DWPose→PSM1 smoke. The official claim launcher found no available local GPU; SSH to the apparently unclaimed `gpu5` stopped at host-key verification. No inference ran, and no result artifact was produced. :codex-annotation{index="1"}
- **Confidence and visibility:** Confirmed tennis pose renderers use a 0.2 visibility threshold and ignore confidence magnitude. The hand demo renderer draws every finite landmark regardless of hand confidence, so its adapter preserves those points and omits the unused score. :codex-annotation{index="2"}
- **Shared motion contract:** Added PSM1 sequence encoding/decoding with schema and image dimensions, frame and object IDs, visibility, quantized coordinates, and GOP resets. The main runner and egocentric demo now reconstruct from decoded coordinates; float16 remains a control. A synthetic eight-frame fixture measured 473 B and 0.318 px mean landmark error for PSM1, versus 729 B and 0.996 px for the legacy hand packets. This is a regression fixture, not dataset or paper evidence. :codex-annotation{index="3"}
- **Racket:** Added an optional cross representation: it references the already-sent player wrist, sends the tip and widest chord, and records wrist-to-tip and chord edges. Missing wrist/geometry falls back to the hull; the hull remains the default pending matched-quality evaluation. :codex-annotation{index="4"}

The affected motion, runner, demo, rigid-object, and schema tests pass, as do scoped Ruff, mypy, and layer checks. Repository-wide mypy still reports 114 errors across 16 files; the focused checks on changed modules pass.

The main checkout has overlapping dirty edits in `src/runner/stages.py` and the documentation, so merge those carefully rather than applying a patch blindly. I separated the changes for review: [code patch](/tmp/pointstream-motion-contract-20260926-code.patch) and [documentation patch](/tmp/pointstream-motion-contract-20260926-docs.patch). The real GPU smoke and matched reconstruction evaluation remain open.
```



I believe side chat 2 changed the dw-pose keypoint system for the racket, in which case, after we obtain the sam 3.1 segmentations for the people and rackets, we should use them to extract keypoints for the people and rackets via the respective most updated algorithms. Having obtained the keypoints too, we can use them to train models. Prepare a plan to obtain a cohesive, unified dataset preparation pipeline, while maintaining single source of truth with the key parts of the codebase that are shared by training and runtime of pointstream, e.g., the dw-pose algorithm that creates dataset priors, should be the same that creates the actual metadata of pointstream runtime, and if they differ on any requirements, such as the runtime requiring speed while the dataset can be run slowly offline, have a common interface and implementation, that both extend with their unique needs. This applies to every part of pointstream of course, it's a best practice of software engineering. The plan should include a test script that can run on a few frames from different scenes, and print results and figures that I can audit.

The goal was pursued for a few hours, but certain tasks were delayed because of a lack of GPU support. I should have solved that, so confirm that, then analyze what the progress since my last prompt is, and report whether all is well and we can continue, or if something was done wrong and should be fixed.

**GPU access is working, and existing-stack experiments can resume. However, the generation path needs repairs before its results can be trusted.**

I verified the RTX A6000 outside the sandbox: 49 GB VRAM, idle at the check, and a successful CUDA computation using PointStream’s PyTorch environment. Sandboxed GPU queries still fail; that failure should not be treated as evidence that the host GPU is unavailable.

The recent work includes real progress:

| Work | Verified status |
|---|---|
| YOLO26x pilot | Real 16-frame PointStream encode/decode. Saved stream, decoded frames, and inspection images match their recorded hashes. |
| AV1/VVC anchor runner | Implemented with process logging and mocked tests; matched experimental results remain unrun. |
| Court geometry scorer | Implemented with tests; endpoint integration and calibration remain unfinished. |
| Generative crop preparation | Useful implementation, but contains a regression and encounters inherited pipeline defects. |

**There is still no new fair baseline win.** The YOLO pilot totals **1,024,847 bytes**, but lacks same-window anchors and a paired SAM comparison. Its cached masks remain imperfect evaluation references.

Three generation problems should be fixed:

1. **New aspect-ratio regression:** AnimateAnyone preparation squeezes a differently shaped target pose into the reference image’s geometry. An existing regression test fails.
2. **Inherited segmentation bypass:** heuristic detector masks can cause the pipeline to skip the actual segmenter. Checking only whether a mask exists does not guarantee proper actor segmentation.
3. **Inherited player mixing:** temporal dispatch can combine different players into one sequence, while AnimateAnyone uses the first appearance as its reference. Sequences need grouping by player.

These issues do **not** invalidate the saved YOLO pilot, which injected measured masks and disabled generation.

Validation is not fully green: the expanded tests exposed the aspect-ratio failure, and full mypy reports **128 errors across 23 files**, including both new and legacy code. Import-direction checks pass.

The earlier categorical rejection of SAM3.1 based on driver 535 was also too strong. NVIDIA permits CUDA 12.x minor-version compatibility with limitations; SAM3.1 needs an isolated runtime and actual kernel/checkpoint test. Its compatibility remains **unverified**. [NVIDIA compatibility documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/cuda-compatibility/minor-version-compatibility.html)

I updated [PLAN.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/PLAN.md), the [experiment plan](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/docs/strategy/journal-experiment-plan.md), and the owning area docs, including the [generation repair findings](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/docs/areas/generation.md:3). No separate handoff was created.

**Proceed with matched AV1/VVC anchors and metric calibration; repair and validate generation before running generator comparisons.** The code defects are documented, not fixed by this audit.

I merged the useful handoff requirements into the current experiment cards and area docs, then removed the separate handoffs, expired dispatch briefs, and stale demo findings and pitch drafts. The dated campaign measurements remain under [docs/history/campaigns](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/docs/history/campaigns/). The egocentric demo pages now clearly mark their comparisons as unvalidated; I did not publish them.

[PLAN.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/PLAN.md) now routes new work through the experiment plan, owning area, setup, and session workflow. The next sequence is R-01 metric calibration and R-02 AV1/VVC parity, followed by the bounded codec search when those gates pass. Current host and learned-checkpoint blockers are recorded in the [experiment plan](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/docs/strategy/journal-experiment-plan.md).

Local Markdown links and `git diff --check` pass. I did not run experiments or alter the existing code edits; the documentation is ready for the next experiment and implementation sessions.

items.text:
**No—not as a verified, paper-ready win over the baselines.** The headline arithmetic is internally consistent, but the experiment does not yet demonstrate that an independent decoder can reconstruct that result from the bytes PointStream claims to transmit.

The JE-10 JSON adds up: 24,648 + 29,088 + 780 + 10,324 = **64,840 B**, and its reported weighted-PSNR calculation reproduces **26.589 dB**, versus **25.366 dB** for the listed VVC QP 46 anchor. The background payload files exist, and the two saved AV1 object streams total 29,088 B. Those are encouraging checks, but they verify the accounting and arithmetic—not the full codec result. [JE-10 result]( /home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/outputs/journal-20260924/je10/alcaraz000-je10-winning-result.json)

The decisive gap is the decode path. The committed JE-10 runner reconstructs using an already-decoded background array and source-derived tracks and masks held in memory. It does not save and then decode a complete PointStream bitstream; the motion and silhouette wires are not persisted in the JE-10 output directory, and the tests check helper behavior and byte arithmetic rather than an end-to-end decode. So the reported quality has not been shown to come from a decoder that receives only the charged payload. Until that is tested, the 309-byte rate advantage and quality advantage are **candidate results**, not a verified codec win.

Other parts of Antigravity’s summary also overstate what the artifacts establish:

- **“Pareto win over baselines” is too broad.** JE-10 reports one Alcaraz clip and one VVC QP 46 point. It does not establish a rate–distortion frontier, a win over AV1, or a win across clips. The foreground stream is reported at 25 fps while the source is documented at 24 fps; that timing discrepancy should be resolved before treating the comparison as fair.
- **JE-11 is an extrapolation, not measured multi-point amortization.** Its JSON applies the same recurring PointStream and VVC costs to successive points; it does not identify distinct point inputs or report per-point quality. The 5- and 10-point savings follow from that repeated-cost assumption. [JE-11 results]( /home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/outputs/journal-20260924/je11/consecutive-points-amortization.json)
- **JE-05 and JE-07 need narrower interpretations.** JE-05’s 12.99 dB Federer figure is pixel PSNR in a heuristic court-line mask, not a measured line-displacement error proving the cause is camera pan. JE-07’s JSON contains conflicting summary and result values for silhouette rate and IoU. [JE-07 results]( /home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-data/outputs/journal-20260924/je07/je07-appearance-silhouette-evaluation.json)
- **The ablations and runtime results do not rescue the main claim.** JE-12’s results are conditional on the unverified JE-10 reconstruction. JE-16 reports 66 seconds of compositing in addition to the shorter decode components, so its client total is not just the background warp, AV1 decode, and silhouette time in the summary.

I ran the committed JE-10 tests from a clean export of `main`; both pass, but they do not exercise full serialization, an independent decoder, or baseline comparison. I also found uncommitted changes in the main checkout and the separate manuscript checkout, so I made no edits that might disturb active work.

I would describe JE-10 as a **promising single-point candidate that needs end-to-end validation**, not as a definitive or journal-ready win. The essential next evidence is a saved, fully accounted PointStream payload that an independent decoder can reconstruct without source-side arrays, followed by matched VVC and AV1 rate–distortion measurements on the same clips and timing.

content.text:
We keep trying to improve pointstream but the results are not satisfactory. Let's start from the basics: the idea of this paper is that traditional codecs waste resources because they don't know what they are encoding, so they have to rely on pixel level compression techniques: DCT, residuals, etc., while humans process visual information much more efficiently, by having mental images of common objects, how they move, etc. so we want to leverage thi semantic knowledge to increase video encoding effiency.



From this idea, we derived that a video is composed of background, which the viewer doesn't look at nor cares about very much, and just needs to be encoded good enough to not distract, and foreground, which is more important to encode well. So we wrote the presley paper (/home/itec/emanuele/presley/68e8b6bb11d0dd9e62a67aef) to compress the background more than the foreground, which gets good results.



To push further, we noticed that for example moving humans are complex for a pixel-level codex to compress, but their movement can be easily modeled by computer vision algorithms, for example by tracking their skeleton keypoints. And we wanted to use this for a new compression algorithm for human motion. So we wrote the genstream paper (/home/itec/emanuele/genstream/682c320f388146ae7ee133b7) to show that compressing an ice skating video where the athlete and the background are known in advance, like at the olympics, is a matter of skeleton keypoints and camera poses, which dramatically reduces bitrate compared to streaming a traditional video.



We then set out to extend this idea to more general tasks, where the background is not available in advance as a 3d model, and we noticed that for many content types, for example sports (but also maybe egocentric video and aerial shots), background is not only less crucial to the viewer, but also slow-changing or anyway composed of a static plate that a camera pans, zooms and tilts around. Traditional codecs need to re-encode the background every segment, and even inside the segment, if the camera moves away from a portion of the background, then returns later, the codec might have to re-encode that portion anew, even though its information is available in a previous frame. So we set out to encode the background as a static plate, with panorama stitching algorithms, and saving the warping matrices, which are invertible and thus allow to reobtain the original frames from the panorama, basically consituting a background encoder. The viewer would lose information about how the background changed over time, but save rate at comparable quality.



We identified tennis point scene as a best case scenario, where two athletes holding rackets are moving in the foreground, without overlapping (which complicates the computer vision tasks of detecting them, their shape, and their skeleton keypoints precisely), and a small ball is dashing between them. The background it also the same for a very long time (hours of a match) and static aside from movements from the audience or ball kids, which are not very relevant. The camera is also mostly static, and only panning and zooming. Our assumption is that leveraging these idiosyncrasies supposedly allows a much higher compression efficiency than traditional streaming, so we set out to implement pointstream, merging the genstream approach to human keypoint compression, with the idiosyncrasies of tennis backgrounds.



So then we needed a model that takes a reference image plus skeleton motion, and turns that into a video of the reference image. We first found [https://huggingface.co/lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-openpose](https://huggingface.co/lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-openpose), which does a seemingly correct but rough job, and has no temporal dimension, so every generation risks being very different from the previous one. We looked into and trained various architectures, from SPADE, to multi-controlnets that use segmentations and canny filters, and finally found [https://github.com/HumanAIGC/AnimateAnyone](https://github.com/HumanAIGC/AnimateAnyone), which seems pretty good from the advertisement and demo, so we have also fine tuned that for tennis. We have kept looking for newer, better models, but found nothing better yet. A possible, untested alternative is MTTF: [https://github.com/\](https://github.com/)xyzysz/Extreme-Human-Video-Compression-with-MTTF](https://github.com/]\(https://github.com/\)xyzysz/Extreme-Human-Video-Compression-with-MTTF). It still compresses keyframes with VVC and generates the inter frames. Reportedly, it does beat VVC on talking faces and moving-body clips, at ultra-low rate, with perceptual as well as objective scores. Broadcast tennis at a PSNR ledger is outside that regime: arbitrary clothing, a racket, a ball, 4K texture. Score Pointstream at ultra low rate, where baselines can't do a good job, with a perceptual metric on the player and a geometric check on the court (line alignment). PSNR or VMAF will keep punishing a deliberately soft crowd and will hide a sharp court.



Unfortunately, surpassing vvc and av1 baselines has proven very difficult for several reasons that we have recorded in detail in the documentation of the project. One that might not have been recorded yet is that each scene paid a new background and appearance crop set, but in theory we don't need the appearance vector for each scene, we can send one appearance and one background at the beginning of the match, and use them for the rest of the match, as they should remain the same while the traditional codecs re-encode them at every segment, drastically reducing bitrate of every following match point to the motion keypoints plus residuals. However, today we found out that VVC and AV1 have "composite long-term reference": The encoder builds one extra picture that is never displayed. Blocks are chosen by a combined cost so that still background is kept and moving foreground is left out, often by blending the clean parts of several frames. That picture is inserted as a long-term reference. Later frames predict from it with ordinary block motion compensation and still send a residual. This is the same background idea as PointStream’s plate, which means we cannot just present it as an advantage over baselines, pretending they couldn't do the same. So we should acknowledge the feature, allow baselines to use it, and should evaluate whether to borrow its strengths into pointstream:

1. Most background blocks stay cached for the match; a block is replaced only when lighting or a ball kid has made it stale. That avoids the bitrate burst of restitching the plate.
2. Combined-cost selection, or a mask, is what keeps the player out of the background picture.



So I asked a Cursor session for advice, and it responded:

1. What the idea got right, and where it stops: The chain from Presley to GenStream to PointStream is coherent. Presley showed that a conventional codec spends a disproportionate share of its bits on a small salient region. GenStream showed that if the decoder already has the athlete and the scene, pose and camera replace the pixel stream. PointStream asked whether that second result survives when the background is not a pre-shared 3D model and the athlete is not a pre-shared renderer. It does not, on broadcast tennis, against VVC, at the quality you are scoring. That is a result, not a failure to finish the implementation.
2. Two different bets got bundled into one codec, and only one of them is real.
   1. Rate allocation is real, and it is modest. Painting the players out and re-encoding saves about 14–18% BD-rate on eight 4K scenes (up to about 27% when the player is large, near zero when the player is small and the camera is fast). That saving *is* the player’s bitrate. Putting the player back at the same quality spends it again. You beat the anchor only if the player comes back for less than those bits. On the 23 September background campaign, the only clip that leaves a usable budget at a matched court is Perricard scene 002: the inpainted video is 86,894 bytes against a 104,482 byte source, so 17,588 bytes remain and the foreground only has to match the anchor’s 24.9 dB. Alcaraz scene 000, nearly still, leaves about 40 kB on a panorama with the court 1.5 dB down, and the foreground has to gain about 0.65 dB. Federer scene 007, the clip the ladder has been living on, leaves 4 kB once the court is matched. A small player plus a pan is the worst case for this idea, and it has been the development clip.
   2. The panorama is not a better background model than VVC. A registered plate on Federer sits around 23–24 dB in the background. The residual of that warp is 107 kB at QP 46 to reach 29.6 dB, still short of the anchor’s 31.4 dB background, and the plate plus residual already exceeds the 112 kB anchor before the players are added. VVC’s block motion compensation is already “static court, camera moved,” and it is a finer motion model than one homography: lens distortion, non-planar stands, audience, ball kids. MPEG-4 sprite coding found the same limit twenty years ago. A single mosaic wins when the camera is still or the warp is nearly exact; it loses once perspective error accumulates, which is why later work split sequences into multi-sprites. The “hours of a match” amortization does not rescue this. The plate is a few tens of kilobytes once. The warp residual is about as large as the entire anchor *per 48 frames*. Paying it every frame never amortizes.
3. Of the 136,228 bytes for one crop plus COCO-17, the keypoints are 4,794 bytes: 47 frames times 102 bytes of raw float16. The crop is 1,962 bytes. About 129 kB is the background plate. Pose is 3.5% of the wire. A couple of pixels of lossy error, and a delta from frame t to frame t+1, can shrink those 4,794 bytes toward 1 kB. That is worth doing, and it does not change the comparison. Deleting the pose stream entirely still leaves a bitstream larger than the VVC anchor, because the plate is the bitstream.
4. The registered-plate experiment treated everything behind the players as one layer. A warped sprite reached about 23.6 dB on that whole background. The residual that pulled it toward the anchor was 107 kB and still short of VVC’s 31.4 dB background, at a total already above the 112 kB anchor. Most of that error is not the court plane. Stands, crowd, ball kids, and shadows are not a plane, so one homography cannot lock them. Judging the warp by full-background PSNR made a good court fit look like a bad background model. Instead, the video can be split into multiple layers:
   1. Class 1, the players: One appearance plus body pose plus two or three racket points (hand, throat, tip). The generator’s job is to move that photographed person. The gap is that the generators you have, including the tennis fine-tune of AnimateAnyone, were not trained to read a throat and a tip, so a racket will still smear until the conditioning includes those points. Pose bytes are already about 5 kB of the old 136 kB stream. Lossy, temporally predicted joints are worth doing, but are unlikely to decide the paper. The sprite and the crowd layer will.
   2. Class 2, the court: On a planar court seen by a fixed-mount camera, a homography is the exact frame-to-frame map, including zoom, as long as the camera center does not translate. A cylinder is the right sprite surface for a horizontal pan: a flat mosaic spends its pixels on stretched corners once the pan is wide, which is the cost Farin cut by splitting sprites. OpenCV’s CylindricalWarper builds that piece. A new sprite when the court warp error jumps is the same rule as his partition. PlaneWarper is what you have now; it is the short-pan special case. Estimate that matrix on a cleaned frame, then apply it to the original pixels. Masking people out of the fit is required, or a player step drags the court. Blurring grass grain before the fit keeps the estimate on the lines and the surface contrast. Undistort first when you have the lens; a long broadcast lens is a small correction, a full-court wide view is not. The sprite is built from the original frames. The only allowed generative step on this layer is a seam cleanup after the warp, not a new court. The ball stays on this layer. A trajectory is a few bytes if the detector holds. A residual is a small window around the ball when it does not. The court residual has to be measured on the court mask alone. If that residual is still tens of kilobytes per point, the cylinder did not lock the plane and another warper will not either. If it is small, the previous 107 kB figure was the crowd, and class 3 is allowed to look soft.
   3. Class 3, everyone else: Umpire, ball kids, line judges, crowd, and stands move or sit off the court plane. One blurred plate, warped by the same camera update as the court, is the cheap version, and it is the right default. A coarse temporal stream is the version you use where that plate is visibly wrong. Generating class 3 at the client side, instead of sending it, saves bits only when done at the once at the start of the match, then gets the same warp as the court.
5. A PSNR win against VVC on a 48-frame 4K window is not available from this design. The journal claim that is still available is narrower, and it matches the original idea: 
   1. For fixed-mount pan-tilt-zoom sports, cache the court and one appearance per player for the match, and transmit temporally coded pose plus a ball trajectory. Reconstruct the players with a pose-conditioned generator. In the ultra-low-rate band, where AV1 and VVC smear both the player and the court, the reconstruction might be preferred on a perceptual metric, because the court stays sharp and the player stays an identifiable person. That is distinct from talking-head codecs. Those generate the whole frame from a face prior. A hallucinated sweater is acceptable there; a hallucinated court line is not. PointStream’s contribution is the split: geometry that must stay exact is cached, appearance that a generator can carry is posed, and the object neither can represent (the ball) is sent explicitly. Presley is the evidence that the player is where the conventional codec spends a disproportionate rate. GenStream is the evidence that pose replaces pixels once appearance is known. PointStream is the broadcast case, where the scene is not pre-modeled in 3D and the camera is a PTZ.
   2. Publish LPIPS at matched ultra-low rate. The operating point is below the current QP 46 anchor, at a resolution the generator was trained for, composited back onto the court.
   3. Count the court and the appearance once, and plot rate against longer and longer scenes, until the curve crosses the baseline anchor.



Couple things missing from the report:

1\. We did not talk about weighted metrics: every layer of the final video will have its own quality, and they don't matter the same, e.g., foreground is more important than audience. What we are trying to maximize is the weighted quality metric. We might even score different layers in different ways: LPIPS for FG, since the generations will not target pixel adherence, but cohesive appearance; geometric line alignment check and VMAF on the court since that's not generated, but warped and thus risks misalignment, etc.

2\. We did not discuss other domains: is tennis even the correct one, given pointstream's strengths and weaknesses compared to baselines?

3\. Would the paper require a neural codec as an additional baseline? What are the tradeoffs expected? The current pointstream demo uses an agocentric video dataset, is that better than tennis for pointstream's chances of being a successful journal paper?



Ask me if anything is unclear, then organize all this content into a new document, that we can reference and update later. Do not read the semantic-codec-thesis.md that Sol produced, it is not a high quality report, delete it before opening it to avoid polluting your context, and create a new one from scratch.
